Below is a verse-by-verse commentary on Jeremiah 44, drawn from the sources I was able to access within the search and fetch limits. Each note is followed by its URL.

---

## Jeremiah 44 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

The chapter records Jeremiah's final recorded prophecy, delivered to the Jewish refugees who had fled to Egypt against God's express command (Jeremiah 42–43). God reminds them that Jerusalem's fall was due to idolatry, confronts their present rebellion in Egypt, and pronounces severe judgment. The people respond with breathtaking defiance, openly declaring they will continue worshipping the "Queen of Heaven." Jeremiah ends with a final prophecy that Pharaoh Hophra will fall to his enemies, serving as a sign that God's words will surely stand. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/ ; Bible.org: https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-44)

---

### vv. 1–6: God Reminds the People of Their Past Sins

**v. 1 — "the word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the Jews living in the land of Egypt—in Migdol, Tahpanhes, and Memphis—and in the land of Pathros"**

- This prophecy was delivered after the Jews had already settled in Egypt. Migdol was near the Red Sea (near Pelusium), Tahpanhes (Daphne) was where the king's palace stood, Noph/Memphis was a major city of Middle Egypt, and Pathros was Upper Egypt (Thebais). The Jews were thus scattered across the length of Egypt. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/44.htm ; Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-44.html)
- The word came "against" or "unto" all the Jews — it was a word of reproof and threatening, not comfort, because they lived in open rebellion. (Trapp, cited in Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)

**v. 2 — "You have seen all the disaster that I brought against Jerusalem... they lie today in ruins and desolation"**

- God opens by reminding the people that the fall of Jerusalem was *His own doing* — "I brought." It was not that He was powerless before Babylon, but that He actively judged His people. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)
- They had seen it with their own eyes; they could not plead ignorance. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/44.htm)
- "No man dwelleth therein" — the desolation of Judah must have been exceedingly great for this to be said of it. (Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-44.html)

**v. 3 — "because of the evil they have done... burning incense and serving other gods that neither they nor you nor your fathers ever knew"**

- The particular sin that provoked God was idolatry — burning incense to and serving other gods. The phrase "whom they knew not" is an aggravation: they abandoned the God who had made Himself known for gods they had no history with and who could not prove themselves to be gods at all. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/44.htm)
- Israel's problem was covenant disobedience: not listening to YHWH and going after other gods. (Bible.org: https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-44)

**v. 4 — "I sent you all My servants the prophets again and again, saying: 'Do not do this detestable thing that I hate'"**

- "Rising early and sending them" is anthropomorphic language used repeatedly in Jeremiah (7:25; 25:4; 26:5; 29:19), picturing God's eager, persistent sending of His messengers. (Ellicott: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/44.htm)
- "Oh, do not do this abominable thing" — Clarke notes the tender entreaty here: God commands, but also pleads as a Father. It is "one of the finest figures of poetry... the anthropopathia." (Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-44.html)
- The term "abominable thing" or "abomination" is characteristic of Deuteronomy, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel when applied to idolatry. (Ellicott: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/44.htm)
- **Spurgeon (Baptist)** is quoted: "Oh! says someone, 'sin is a sweet thing.' No, no; it is an abominable thing... Though it should crawl up to a monarch's throne, and spread its slime over crown jewels it would still be an abominable thing." (Cited in Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)
- **Matthew Henry** adds: "It becomes us to speak of sin with the utmost dread and detestation... Call it grievous, call it odious... If you love God, do not, for it is provoking to him; if you love your own souls, do not, for it is destructive to them." (Matthew Henry, via Bible Hub search excerpt: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/44.htm)

**v. 5 — "But they did not listen or incline their ears; they did not turn from their wickedness or stop burning incense to other gods"**

- The people's sin was compounded by their refusal to be corrected. The idolatry was bad; the unteachability was fatal. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)
- Clarke notes four aggravations: they disregarded God's authority, were unmoved by His entreaties, delighted in abominations, and loved what God hated — apparently *because* He hated it. (Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-44.html)

**v. 6 — "Therefore My wrath and anger poured out and burned... so that they have become the desolate ruin they are today"**

- The fall of Judah was not because Marduk or Babylon was strong, but because of Judah's covenant disobedience. YHWH brought the curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 27–30 to bear. (Bible.org: https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-44)
- "My fury and mine anger was poured forth" — like melted metal or liquefied pitch, spreading, consuming, and intolerable. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/44.htm)

---

### vv. 7–10: God Confronts Their Present Sin in Egypt

**v. 7 — "Why are you doing such great harm to yourselves by cutting off from Judah man and woman, child and infant, leaving yourselves without a remnant?"**

- There is a sense of wonder in God's question — as though He cannot believe their folly so soon after witnessing Jerusalem's devastation. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)
- "This great evil against your souls" — sin is self-destructive. Will not self-interest weigh with you? (Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-44.html)
- "Against yourselves" is key: they were sinning against God, yes, but also terribly against themselves and their posterity. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)

**v. 8 — "provoking Me to anger... burning incense to other gods in the land of Egypt, where you have gone to reside"**

- The exiles were not only continuing old idolatrous practices but had adopted those of Egypt. This was exactly what Jeremiah and Isaiah before him had always feared about alliances with Egypt. (Ellicott: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/44.htm)
- The same heart of idolatry that led them to sin in Judah with Canaanite idols now led them to Egyptian idols. This reveals why God commanded them not to go there. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)
- "That you may cut yourselves off and be a curse and a reproach among all the nations" — the covenant people were meant to be a blessing to the nations (Gen. 12:3), but they had become a curse. (Bible.org: https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-44)

**v. 9 — "Have you forgotten the wickedness of your fathers and of the kings of Judah and their wives, as well as the wickedness that you and your wives committed"**

- The question is rhetorical: they *had* forgotten. The mention of "their wives" and "your wives" highlights the prominent role women played in idolatry, particularly in the worship of the "Queen of Heaven." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/ ; Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-44.html)
- Gill notes that "the wickedness of his wives" in the Hebrew could refer particularly to Solomon's wives, who drew him into idolatry, or distributively to the wives of each king. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/44.htm)

**v. 10 — "To this day they have not humbled themselves or shown reverence, nor have they followed My instruction"**

- The verb "humbled" (Hebrew *dukke'u*) means literally "bruised" or "crushed" — there was no contrition, no brokenness over sin. (Feinberg, cited in Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/ ; Bible.org: https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-44)
- The shift from "you" to "they" in the Hebrew suggests God no longer addresses the impenitent directly but speaks *about* them — a sign of judicial distance. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/44.htm)

---

### vv. 11–14: The Promise of Judgment on Those Who Went to Egypt

**v. 11 — "I will set My face to bring disaster and to cut off all Judah"**

- "I will set My face against you" is vocabulary from Leviticus 26 (the covenant curses). YHWH will personally bring judgment. (Bible.org: https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-44)
- There is a grim symmetry: they "set their faces" to go to Egypt (v. 12), so God sets His face against them. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/44.htm ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)

**v. 12 — "I will take away the remnant of Judah who have resolved to go to the land of Egypt... they will meet their end"**

- God distinguishes between two groups of exiles: those taken to Babylon would be blessed and restored; those who by their own choice went to Egypt would face only judgment. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)
- "They shall be an execration, and an astonishment, and a curse, and a reproach" — the same formula used in Jeremiah 42:18. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/44.htm ; Bible.org: https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-44)

**v. 13 — "I will punish those who live in the land of Egypt, just as I punished Jerusalem, by sword and famine and plague"**

- The same judgments that fell on Jerusalem would fall on Egypt-dwelling Jews. They fled to Egypt thinking they would escape, but judgment followed them. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/44.htm)
- This points to a punishment on all Egypt, from which the Jews dwelling there would find no exemption. (Ellicott: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/44.htm)

**v. 14 — "none of the remnant of Judah who have gone to reside in Egypt will escape or survive to return... except a few fugitives"**

- "To the which they have a desire to return" — literally, "unto which they lift up their souls to return." The exiles still cherished the hope of returning to Judah. (Ellicott: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/44.htm)
- God promises a tiny remnant will escape — enough to maintain the connection between the people and the land, but precious few. (Harrison, cited in Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)
- "Egypt was not in itself forbidden territory... The sin of Jeremiah's contemporaries was not geographical; it was a vote of no confidence in God." (Kidner, cited in Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)

---

### vv. 15–19: The People's Defiant Response

**v. 15 — "Then all the men who knew that their wives were burning incense to other gods, and all the women standing by—a great assembly"**

- This is a striking scene: "a great multitude" of both men and women, assembled and answering the prophet together. The inclusive language ("all the men," "all the women") is a literary generalization for emphasis. (Feinberg, cited in Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)
- The men "knew" their wives were burning incense — they winked at it and did not restrain them as they ought. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/44.htm)
- Clarke notes: "We have not seen the women in determined rebellion before. Here they make a common cause with their idolatrous husbands." (Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-44.html)

**v. 16 — "As for the word you have spoken to us in the name of the LORD, we will not listen to you!"**

- The people openly rejected Jeremiah's word *even while acknowledging* he spoke in the name of the LORD. Their honesty is remarkable; their sin is breathtaking. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)
- Gill calls this "an unparalleled instance of the pride, obstinacy, enmity, and rebellion of the carnal mind against God." (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/44.htm)
- The Baptist Garner-Howes Commentary says: "In essence, they told him that he might as well save his breath; they had no intention of giving heed to his words." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-44.html)

**v. 17 — "Instead, we will do everything we vowed to do: We will burn incense to the Queen of Heaven and offer drink offerings to her"**

- "The Queen of Heaven" (*melecheth hashamayim*) is probably the Assyro-Babylonian Ishtar (Canaanite Athtart/Astarte, Greek Astarte), goddess of war, love, and fertility. She was associated with the planet Venus and the moon. Her counterpart in the NT is Artemis (Diana) of Ephesus (Acts 19). (Feinberg, cited in Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)
- Clarke identifies her specifically with the moon: "The MOON seems to have been called מלכת *melecheth*, as the SUN was called מלך *molech*." (Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-44.html)
- The people justified their idolatry by appealing to antiquity, authority, and prosperity: "we, our fathers, our kings, and our officials did it... and we had plenty." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)
- **Matthew Henry** draws a pointed application: "All who worship images, or honour saints, and angels, and the queen of heaven, should recollect what came from the idolatrous practices of the Jews." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/44.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Pentecostal/Evangelical)** makes an explicitly anti-Catholic application: "It is strange and shocking that Roman Catholics give Mary, the mother of Jesus, this same title and direct to her improper prayer and veneration – sometimes even worship. We have no Biblical permission or encouragement to have any connection with the queen of heaven." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)

**v. 18 — "But from the time we stopped burning incense to the Queen of Heaven... we have lacked everything and have been perishing by sword and famine"**

- "This is a most revealing glimpse of spiritual perversity — for in blaming all their troubles on the reformation instead of on the evils it had tried to root out, these people were turning the truth exactly upside down." (Kidner, cited in Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)
- The people were referring to Josiah's reforms (2 Kings 23:4–20), when Baal and Asherah worship was suppressed. They blamed their subsequent troubles on *stopping* the idolatry, rather than on the idolatry itself. (Harrison, cited in Enduring Word; Garner-Howes: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-44.html)
- The long and relatively peaceful reign of wicked king Manasseh (55 years) may have been the "good old days" they remembered, when idolatry flourished freely. (Thompson, cited in Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)
- Ellicott notes the parallel with Roman arguments when calamity fell on the Empire — pagans blamed Christians for abandoning the old gods (Tertullian, *Apology* ch. 40; Augustine, *City of God* I.36). (Ellicott: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/44.htm)

**v. 19 — "Moreover," said the women, "when we burned incense to the Queen of Heaven... was it without our husbands' knowledge that we made sacrificial cakes in her image?"**

- The women defend themselves by saying their husbands knew and approved. They made crescent-shaped cakes (*kawwan*) stamped with the image of the goddess, and their husbands did not stop them. (Thompson, cited in Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)
- Under Numbers 30:3–12, a woman's vow was binding only if her husband approved it. The women's argument was: "Since our husbands approved, why should Jeremiah complain?" (Feinberg, cited in Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)
- **Ellicott** notes: "We have here, it is obvious, the very words of the women who were stung by what they looked on as Jeremiah's intimation that the chief guilt lay on them. They disclaim any special responsibility." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/44.htm)
- The Enduring Word commentary adds that the women were still guilty — submission to husbands does not extend to obeying them in sin. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)

---

### vv. 20–23: Jeremiah's Rebuttal — Why Destruction Really Came

**v. 21 — "did the LORD not remember and bring this to mind?"**

- Jeremiah reasons with the people: they had completely left God out of their thinking. They assumed that if they ignored God, He didn't matter. But He saw and remembered everything. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)

**v. 22 — "So the LORD could no longer endure the evil deeds and detestable acts you committed, and your land became a desolation"**

- God was very patient, but they mistook His patience for indifference. "His abused mercy turned into fury." (Trapp, cited in Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)
- The prosperity of past years had not been lasting — though God's long-suffering bore with them, judgment finally came. (Ellicott: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/44.htm)

**v. 23 — "Because you burned incense and sinned against the LORD... this disaster has befallen you"**

- The cause-and-effect is crystal clear: covenant disobedience produced covenant curses. The people's own interpretation of events (vv. 17–18) was exactly wrong. (Bible.org: https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-44)
- Matthew Henry: "The right understanding of the cause of our troubles, one would think, should go far towards the cure of our sins. Whatever evil comes upon us, it is because we have sinned against the Lord." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/44.htm)

---

### vv. 24–30: Final Judgment and a Sign

**v. 25 — "Go ahead, then, do what you have promised! Keep your vows!"**

- There is a powerful tone of irony and revulsion here. Jeremiah tells them to proceed with fulfilling their godless vows — since they are determined, let them do it. It echoes Ezekiel 20:39: "Go, serve every one of you his idols." (Feinberg, cited in Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/ ; Garner-Howes: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-44.html)
- The people's vows to the Queen of Heaven use the same emphatic Hebrew construction (infinitive absolute + imperfect verb) that God will use to declare His judgment — a rhetorical mirror. (Bible.org: https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-44)

**v. 26 — "never again will any man of Judah living in the land of Egypt invoke My name or say, 'As surely as the Lord GOD lives'"**

- God swears by His own "great name" — matching oath for oath. The people swore by the Queen of Heaven; God swears by His name that they will lose the right even to speak it. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)
- Gill notes: "He forbids them to swear by His holy name!" It is a judicial exclusion from covenant relationship. (Gill, via search excerpt; Garner-Howes: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-44.html)

**v. 27 — "I am watching over them for harm and not for good"**

- The verb "watching over" (*shoqed*) is the same theological word used in Jeremiah 1:12 ("I am watching over My word to perform it") and 31:28 — God's focused attention can be for blessing or for judgment. Here it is for judgment. (Bible.org: https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-44)
- God had promised to watch over them for good if they stayed in Judah and trusted Him. By rejecting that, they now have God watching over them for adversity — a terrifying reversal. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)

**v. 28 — "Those who escape the sword will return from Egypt to Judah, few in number, and... will know whose word will stand, Mine or theirs!"**

- A small remnant will survive to return — just enough to prove God's word true and to maintain the connection between people and land. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)
- The question "whose word will stand" is the ultimate challenge: the defiant words of rebels or the sure word of YHWH? (Bible.org: https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-44)

**v. 29 — "This will be a sign to you... so that you may know that My threats of harm against you will surely stand"**

- "My words will surely stand" uses the same emphatic Hebrew construction (infinitive absolute + imperfect) that was used for the idolaters' vows in v. 25. God matches their certainty with His own. (Bible.org: https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-44)

**v. 30 — "Behold, I will deliver Pharaoh Hophra king of Egypt into the hands of his enemies... just as I delivered Zedekiah king of Judah"**

- Pharaoh Hophra (Apries in Herodotus) reigned 588–569 BC. He was the Pharaoh who encouraged Zedekiah to rebel against Babylon and sent troops during the siege of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 37:5). (Bible.org: https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-44 ; Ellicott: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/44.htm)
- Historically, Hophra's general Amasis rebelled against him and was proclaimed king. Hophra was deposed, kept prisoner at Sais, and later strangled. This occurred around 569 BC, fulfilling Jeremiah's prophecy. (Ellicott: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/44.htm ; Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-44.html)
- This was Jeremiah's last recorded prophecy. "He ended as he started: faithful to God, trusting in God's faithfulness... his utter faith in an omnipotent God, and his perception of fundamental truths, are as clear as ever." (Cundall, cited in Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)
- A late Christian tradition (Tertullian, Jerome) holds that the Egyptian Jews, enraged by Jeremiah's reproaches, stoned him to death. Hebrews 11:37 ("they were stoned") may allude to this. (Ellicott: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/44.htm)

---

## Traditions Compared

### On the "Queen of Heaven" (vv. 17–19, 25)

- **Evangelical/Pentecostal (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Strongly identifies the Queen of Heaven as the Babylonian Ishtar and explicitly warns that Roman Catholics give the same title to Mary, calling it "strange and shocking" and "improper prayer and veneration — sometimes even worship." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)
- **Matthew Henry (Reformed/Evangelical):** Makes a similar though less strident application: "All who worship images, or honour saints, and angels, and the queen of heaven, should recollect what came from the idolatrous practices of the Jews." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/44.htm)
- **Clarke (Methodist/Wesleyan):** Identifies the Queen of Heaven straightforwardly as the moon, noting the parallel with Hindu worship practices of pouring out water to the sun and moon. No anti-Catholic polemic. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-44.html)
- **Ellicott (Anglican):** Takes a more academic approach, identifying the crescent-shaped cakes and comparing the people's argument to pagan Roman complaints against Christianity in Tertullian and Augustine. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/44.htm)

### On the Role of Women (v. 19)

- **Clarke:** Holds that "the women were principal agents in idolatrous practices" — the queens and wives of rulers and common people alike. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-44.html)
- **Ellicott:** Notes the women were "stung" by Jeremiah's implication that they bore chief guilt, and they attempted to shift responsibility to their husbands, citing the principle from Numbers 30 that vows required husbandly approval. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/44.htm)
- **Enduring Word:** Agrees the women were genuinely guilty; submission to husbands does not extend to obeying them in sin. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)

### On Jeremiah's Final Ministry (v. 30)

- **Ellicott (Anglican):** Records the early church tradition (Tertullian, Jerome) that Jeremiah was stoned to death by the Egyptian Jews. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/44.htm)
- **Enduring Word:** Emphasises that Jeremiah "ended as he started: faithful to God" despite seeing his nation decline from strength to near extinction with little visible fruit from his ministry. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-44/)
- **Clarke:** Provides the detailed historical fulfillment from Herodotus — Amasis's rebellion, the civil war, Nebuchadnezzar's invasion, and Hophra's eventual strangulation. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-44.html)

The notes above are drawn from the sources that were reachable.
